name: Sahti
description: Finland's living-fossil farmhouse ale: rye and juniper, strained through a hollowed spruce trough, never boiled and never hopped much. Banana, juniper and bread.
funFact: Sahti is unboiled and unfiltered, so it stays cloudy and perishable — it is one of the very few beer styles the EU has granted protected traditional status, and it barely travels.

serve.how: Pour gently into a mug and expect almost no head — sahti is nearly still, and a big foam would mean something went wrong. Serve it cool rather than cold so the banana esters and juniper resin come forward together; ice-cold sahti tastes like flat bread. Drink it fresh, within days if you can, because there is no boil and no real hop cover to protect it.

composition.summary: An unboiled rye-and-barley farmhouse ale flavoured and filtered by juniper.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a large proportion of rye, sometimes oats.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Almost none — juniper branches do the preserving and seasoning instead.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Traditionally baker's yeast, fermented warm, which is where the banana comes from.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Fresh juniper twigs and berries, used both as flavour and as the filter bed.

composition.process: The mash is lautered through juniper branches laid in a hollowed log trough, then fermented warm with baker's yeast and drunk young without boiling.

name: Gotlandsdricka
description: Sahti's Swedish cousin from the island of Gotland: smoked malt, juniper and a farmhouse yeast character, brewed at home for centuries and almost nowhere else.
funFact: Gotland farmers brewed it for holidays and haymaking under a customary right that survived Sweden's alcohol monopoly; the recipes stayed inside families rather than breweries.

serve.how: Serve it cool and still, in a mug rather than a glass, and expect a hazy amber pour with very little foam. Let it sit a minute so the smoke settles behind the juniper instead of dominating it. Like sahti it is meant to be drunk young and local, so treat a bottle as perishable rather than something to age.

composition.summary: A smoked, juniper-infused farmhouse ale from Gotland, fermented warm with a farmhouse yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Home-smoked barley malt, often with rye and a little honey.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Sparing — juniper carries most of the seasoning.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Farmhouse or baker's yeast worked warm, giving spice and stone fruit.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Juniper branches for both flavour and lautering.

composition.process: Malt is dried over an open wood fire, mashed and strained through juniper, then fermented warm and served within weeks.

name: Maltøl
description: Norwegian farmhouse ale fermented with kveik — a hardy house yeast pitched blisteringly hot that finishes clean in two days and tastes of orange and stone fruit.
funFact: Kveik yeast was kept alive on dried wooden rings passed down through Norwegian farm families for generations; when brewers rediscovered it in the 2010s it changed brewing worldwide, because it ferments cleanly at 35–40°C.

serve.how: Pour into a wide vessel and give it a moment — the aroma is the point, and kveik throws citrus and stone fruit that a narrow glass hides. Serve cool rather than cold, since the warmth of the ferment leaves a rounded malt body that goes flat and thin under refrigeration. Traditionally it is passed around a shared bowl rather than poured into individual glasses.

composition.summary: A strong, juniper-tinged farmhouse ale fermented very warm with heritage kveik yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt, often with a caramelised or long-boiled wort for colour.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal, with juniper infusion standing in for much of the character.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Kveik — a heritage farmhouse culture pitched at 35–40°C that finishes in days.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Juniper infusion water used for mashing and sparging.

composition.process: Mashed with juniper infusion, sometimes with a long caramelising boil, then fermented hot with kveik and drunk fresh.

name: Koduõlu
description: Estonian island home-brew: unboiled, juniper-strained and fermented warm, closer to liquid rye bread than to anything on a modern taplist.
funFact: On Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, koduõlu was brewed for weddings and midsummer by designated village brewers, and the tradition survived the Soviet period largely because it was never commercial.

serve.how: Serve cool and flat in a mug — carbonation is minimal and a head is not expected. Give it a few minutes out of the cold so the bready malt and juniper open up; too cold and all you get is sourness. It is brewed to be drunk within days of being made, so freshness matters more than any serving detail.

composition.summary: An unboiled Estonian farmhouse ale strained through juniper and fermented warm.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with rye, often home-malted.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Very low, sometimes none at all.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Farmhouse or baker's yeast, warm-fermented for banana and spice.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Juniper branches in the lauter and juniper water in the mash.

composition.process: Mashed, strained through juniper without boiling, fermented warm for a couple of days and served young.

name: Kaimiškas
description: Lithuania's village farmhouse beer: unfiltered, raw, and fermented with a house yeast that leaves it honeyed and faintly tart. The northern Biržai region is its heartland.
funFact: Lithuanian farmhouse brewing survived unbroken through the twentieth century, which makes it one of the few living raw-ale traditions in Europe; Biržai alone has a cluster of legally operating village breweries.

serve.how: Pour into a plain glass and expect haze and a soft, low carbonation. Serve cool but not cold so the honeyed malt and the faint lactic edge stay in balance. These beers are raw — never boiled — so drink them fresh and do not expect the shelf stability of a modern lager.

composition.summary: A raw, unboiled Lithuanian village ale fermented with a local farmhouse yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt, often with a portion of unmalted grain.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low, boiled separately as a tea and added rather than boiled in the wort.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Regional farmhouse strains that finish honeyed and lightly tart.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nothing beyond the grain — this is a deliberately plain beer.

composition.process: The wort is not boiled; hops are added as a separate infusion, and fermentation runs warm with a house culture before the beer is served young.

name: Keptinis
description: Lithuanian baked beer: the mash is shaped into loaves, baked in a bread oven until dark, then brewed. Tastes of crust, caramel and smoke without any smoked malt.
funFact: The baking step replaces a kiln — the mash literally goes into the oven as loaves before being returned to water, which is why keptinis tastes roasted despite using pale malt.

serve.how: Serve cool in a mug so the bread-crust aroma comes off the surface. Expect a dark, hazy beer with modest carbonation and a long toasty finish. It rewards slow drinking at cellar temperature; cold suppresses exactly the baked-crust character that makes it worth brewing this way.

composition.summary: A farmhouse ale whose mash is baked into loaves before brewing, giving deep crust flavour.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt, transformed by baking rather than by kilning.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low, added as an infusion in the farmhouse manner.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lithuanian farmhouse yeast, warm-fermented.

components.label: Other
components.detail: The oven itself — the baking step is the defining ingredient.

composition.process: The mash is formed into loaves and baked until dark, then broken back into hot water, lautered, and fermented warm without a conventional boil.
